title: Linear systems: conjugate gradient vs the HHL quantum algorithm (conjectured exponential speedup, with fine print and low-rank dequantization)
problem_statement: Given an N x N sparse Hermitian matrix A with condition number kappa, accessible through an oracle for its nonzero entries, and a vector b available as a quantum state |b> (or, classically, by its entries), estimate an expectation value x^T M x of the solution x of Ax = b for a given operator M (HHL's formulation: 'one doesn't need to know the solution x itself, but rather an approximation of the expectation value of some operator associated with x'), to precision eps.

input.parameter: N = dimension; also the sparsity s (nonzeros per row), the condition number kappa and the precision eps.
input.size_measure: Implicit input: A and b are given by efficient access procedures (sparse-entry oracle and state preparation), so the description size is poly(log N, s); an explicit input would already have size Theta(N s).

algorithms.name: classical conjugate-gradient-type solver
algorithms.idea: Krylov-subspace iteration with sparse matrix-vector products; computes x and hence x^T M x.
algorithms.pseudocode: conjugate gradient (for positive definite A; general A via the normal equations or Hermitian embedding)
algorithms.time_complexity: O(N sqrt(kappa)) for sparse A, as stated in the HHL abstract (dependence on s and eps not shown there)
algorithms.correctness: Standard numerical linear algebra; the bound is the one HHL quote as the best classical algorithm.

algorithms.name: HHL quantum algorithm
algorithms.idea: Phase estimation of e^(-iAt) on |b> writes A's eigenvalues into a register; a controlled rotation multiplies each eigencomponent by 1/lambda; uncomputing phase estimation and post-selecting yields |x> proportional to A^(-1)|b>, from which x^T M x is estimated.
algorithms.time_complexity: poly(log N, kappa) (HHL abstract); Aaronson 2015 summarises it as roughly log(N) * kappa * s / eps, given fast preparation of |b> and fast application of e^(-iAt)
algorithms.space_complexity: O(log N) qubits plus phase-estimation and ancilla registers

algorithms.name: quantum-inspired classical algorithm for LOW-RANK A (dequantization; a different input model)
algorithms.idea: With length-squared sampling access to A and b, subsample to an approximate low-rank SVD, invert the singular values, and output samples from or entries of the pseudo-inverse solution.
algorithms.pseudocode: Chia, Lin & Wang 2018; Gilyen, Lloyd & Tang 2018; framework in Chia et al. 2022
algorithms.time_complexity: O(poly(k, kappa, ||A||_F, 1/eps) polylog(m, n)) for a rank-k m x n matrix (Chia, Lin & Wang 2018 abstract): polylogarithmic in the dimension, polynomial in rank, condition number and 1/eps
algorithms.space_complexity: a sampling data structure over A and b (assumed given, like QRAM on the quantum side)
algorithms.correctness: Chia, Lin & Wang 2018; Gilyen, Lloyd & Tang 2018; Chia et al. 2022 (which recovers and often improves 'low-rank regression' among other dequantization results).

lower_bounds.bound: no algorithm in time poly(log N, kappa, 1/eps) for the general sparse well-conditioned case unless every quantum polynomial-time computation can be simulated classically (BQP = BPP)
lower_bounds.setting: CONDITIONAL (on BQP != BPP), not a proven query lower bound; follows from HHL's result that the problem is universal for quantum computation (BQP-complete): any quantum circuit on n qubits can be encoded as a linear system of about 2^n equations
lower_bounds.source: Harrow, Hassidim & Lloyd 2009; universality statement as summarised by Aaronson 2015

relationship: CONJECTURED exponential speedup, not a proven separation: classical O(N sqrt(kappa)) vs quantum poly(log N, kappa) for estimating x^T M x, under strong input assumptions. TAG DECISION: T6 (open / unpaired), not T9 and not T5. Not T9, because no unconditional classical lower bound is known for HHL's task; the only barrier is conditional (HHL's BQP-completeness: a classical poly(log N, kappa, 1/eps) algorithm would give BQP = BPP). Not T5, because the dequantization results apply to LOW-RANK matrices with length-squared sampling access, a different problem and input model from HHL's sparse, full-rank, oracle-access setting, for which no dequantization is known. So, like integer factoring, this is a problem where the best known classical algorithm is exponentially slower in log N than a quantum one, with no proof either way. The low-rank variant belongs with staging/recommendation-systems-dequantization (T5).

verification.method: Cited from the literature. DOIs, titles, years, volumes and issues checked against Crossref; the HHL complexity statements checked against the HHL arXiv abstract (0811.3171); the four caveats and the universality (BQP-completeness) summary checked against Aaronson's preprint of the Nature Physics article; the dequantization bounds checked against the arXiv abstracts of 1811.04852, 1811.04909 and 1910.06151.

caveats: Aaronson (2015) lists four caveats, each of which can remove the speedup: (1) b must be loaded quickly as the state |b>, e.g. from a quantum RAM, and b must be fairly uniform or come with suitable auxiliary data; (2) e^(-iAt) must be applicable quickly, e.g. for sparse A with its nonzero entries in a quantum RAM; (3) A must be robustly invertible: the running time grows nearly linearly with kappa, so kappa ~ N^c kills the speedup; (4) the output is the quantum state |x>, not x: measuring it reveals limited statistics, and reading a specific entry x_i generally needs about N repetitions. He also stresses that the fair comparison is with the best classical algorithm for the same restricted task (estimating observables of x for systems HHL can handle), which may be much faster than O(N sqrt(kappa)); that the instances produced by the universality reduction are 'extremely artificial'; and that the quantum RAM must be passive, since otherwise classical parallelism solves Ax = b in O(log^2 N) steps. The dequantized algorithms likewise assume a preprocessed sampling data structure; their polynomial degrees are large.
notes: Evidence on both sides of the classical-vs-quantum question: a BQP-complete problem (so an exponential speedup exists for SOME instances if BQP != BPP), whose practically motivated low-rank instances were dequantized. Not implemented: simulating HHL on lib/qsim.py would need phase estimation and Hamiltonian simulation and would not measure a query separation.
